“Trash Humpers” is Korine’s most effective work because it’s the one that dares to be what so many of the other ones promise, hint at glancingly and hedge their bets around — deliberately boring, stupid, ugly, dumb — in the most authentically pranksterish punk rock fashion of truly giving no fucks. It’s like if experimental noise rock were someone’s home movies, the cinematic equivalent of “Metal Machine Music.” 

This isn’t pleasant or conventionally engaging to watch. It’s an endurance test meant to be braved and survived.

I’ve seen this relatively short feature repel audiences, drive them from the theater with only 10 minutes left. The director would be proud of that, no doubt, and he should be.

Kids and Gummo were two classic films of my teens, I see them differently now as an adult, but theyre still great films. I think hes best when he narrowly foucses on some kind of fringe/subculture element.

Oh boy. What can I say about Gummo? It is a fever dream of a movie. It is not for the faint of heart as it is highly exploitative. A lot of the cast were just people he hired off the street and I don't think a lot of them were really cognizant of what they were getting involved in. There are a lot of scenes of cat murder, so if animal cruelty is a deal breaker then you might want to skip this. They don't actually kill any real cats, they're props but they look convincing (there is one scene where they do film an actual dead cat, but I think it's some roadkill they found and not one they actually killed). It's a bleak movie and gets pretty gross at times. Like unsanitary gross, not blood and guts. 

A lot of the movie is shock value, but I can argue with the fact that Korine is a competent film maker at least in composition. But storywise, I can't really figure out what kind of statement he is trying to make with this one. The director's comentary doesn't yeild much in the way of an explanation either. I think the lack of a coheirent narrative is probably by design. And I can't be buggered to research it myself.

You will not be bored, I can say that much at least. Just don't expect to make a lot of sense out of it.

We studied it as an example of 'post modern' and 'queer' cinema so it shows an aimlessness, ennui. A lack of meaning to our lives which can't be filled by the consumer driven, neo liberal order so people drift along much like the adolescents in the film...

I liked Spring Breakers and found it uncomfortable in a good way. The ski masks and bikinis were like a twisted American dream carousing from criminal proceeds. James Franco seems a sleazy person and is a good fit for the character to serve the work. The repetition of phases was soulless and made sense as a satire/critique of the culture.

I know a lot of people didn't like it but The Beach Bum is a Top 10 movie for me and I've watched it at least once a year since it came out. In a lot of ways Korine seemed to be subverting himself with that one, creating a glaring positive and life-affirming experience (while still being very weird and singular of vision) And since The Beach Bum also takes place in a neon-soaked hyperreal version of Florida, it plays almost as a yin to Spring Breakers more nihilistic yang.

As a teenager, you watch a Harmony Korine movie and you’re like “holy shit!” Either fascinated or disturbed. 

As an adult, I see what a self-inflating exploitative shitbird creep he is, and it’s hard to divorce that from his work. 

He’s the kind of guy who pretends at “auteur” and will make a film to “make a point” about exploitation or appropriation, for instance, and happily, excessively exploit the actors and characters to present that so-called admonition. 

He never seems to really understand or care about the message of his films, his goal seems only to be playing the role of artist, and excusing himself to do the things he claims to be criticizing.  

I honestly see his work as too on-the-nose, it tries to be extreme to ply the viewer for a certain reaction, and I think that’s effective on teenagers, but for older people like myself, you see the puppet strings and it takes you out of it. 

It’s almost like the difference between torture porn vs a horror film that may have some gore or a gruesome scene or two. 

The latter can be viscerally disturbing and truly horrifying, deep into your bones, fill you with dread. The former not only risks taking you out of the experience, bc you know what’s happening here, it also can take you out of the experience bc of the porn-adjacent disturbing implications of why a person would create such a thing. 

In my opinion, if you want authentically depressing, a movie that clenches your stomach the whole way through, is wholly moving and leaves you crushed at the end, watch Midnight Cowboy. 

If you want viscerally disturbing, watch David Lynch, watch Erasurehead. 

If you want upsetting, watch Elephant Man. 

Basically, I think there are a lot of films that do what Harmony Korine tries to turbo-charge, but in a much more authentic and effective way, without creating a parody of “fucked up.” If that makes sense?

For me, your comment applies much more to Larry Clark, who people tend to confuse with Harmony Korine because it was Clark who directed Kids, while Korine only wrote the screenplay.      
     
Clark's movies have this voyeuristic, ogling aspect to them when he observes teenagers. He's like the sad, older dude who never grew up and still hangs around teens. Ken Park looks like an excuse to shoot nude scenes with young people.      
     
I find Harmony Korine to be very critical of teenagers and how modern culture reveres youth. His characters are trapped in hedonism, but he exposes that sensation-seeking as shallow. Come to think of it, James Franco's character in Spring Breakers is how I see Larry Clark, an older guy leading teens down a destructive path.

Personally Korine films grate on me and seem deliberately nasty and exploitative.I find him so button pushing not for artistic reasons but just because it will give him notoriety. Spring breakers had the girls carelessly twirling around uzi's like they were hair dryer and hard core gang bangers just all collapsing 100 of years away. It was so insanely stupid.
I’ve only seen Gummo and my cat was not a fan. He doesn’t usually watch films with us, but stayed for almost the entirety of a four movie marathon. The last film was Gummo and he left in minutes.

This is the film that made me realize that Harmony Korine is pretty similar to John Waters. They both make transgressive movies about weird and 'perverted' people. I like how Trash Humpers feels like watching a strange VHS home video you found in a forest near you, lol. There's something creepy yet hilarious about it.

You may be right that Clark is worse than Korine, but Korine is writing this stuff and repeatedly presenting it. Spring Breakers wasn’t commentary, it simply masqueraded as such while doing the exact things it claimed to revile. Time and again, this is what emerges from Korine’s work. The only consistent thread is Korine himself. 

So while others may be complicit, it would be illogical to give Korine a pass. This is his MO.

For all the disturbing themes, I actually think his films have a lot of humour in them. He is also a very funny dude if you watch his interviews. You never know if he is bullshitting or not, either way he has a unique charisma. 

You could view him as less film director and more a multidisciplinary artist, which is why maybe he comes off as pretentious to some.

Clearly there are people here who aren’t a fan but my partner is a big fan. 

His older work, (mind you, he was a teenager when he made Gummo) could be described as a series of character vignettes that prioritise atmosphere and “vibe”. Gummo would fit this. 

His film, Julien Donkey Boy, was his Dogme 95 film, which was an avant-garde filmmaking movement in Denmark. 

He is also a painter and artist, he made lots of video pieces for galleries and exhibitions. His later films are heavily influenced by his living in Florida. At the moment he seems to be interested by new media, gaming and the ways people interact with art and technology. 

Overall I think his film making endeavours have always been experimental at its core trying to find new cinematic languages. Agro Drift being such a work I can confidently say, is totally unlike anything I’ve personally experienced.

This I agree with: ''He never seems to really understand or care about the message of his films'', but I think a lot of what you say is a mischaracterization/your own projection of his goals. 
Harmony Korine trying to make a point? What point? Claiming to criticize something? Like what? Plying the viewer for a certain reaction? His work being on-the-nose?  
He has said often he doesn't care about narrative cinema. To him his cinema appears to be (pursuing) moods, ideas, entertainment, colours, images all merging into something musical, weird, interesting and 'cool'. There is very little, if any, judgement, only the pure revelling..
I mean, my humble opinion, but his films Gummo and Julien Donkey Boy, and his book Crack-Up at the Race Riots, are all pretty amazing. He may not be everyone’s cup of tea, but he’s a brave artist.

I'm seeing exploitative being bandied about a lot here, implying that Korine is capitalizing on other's pains, struggles, hard situtations without empathy or any motive beyond creating a shocking film, which I think is a pretty shallow read.  
  
Gummo is a collage of what it is to be "white trash" poor, and poorer than just counting pennies. A deep poverty-level of poor where your neighbors are drug addicts or disabled or exconvicts or otherwise outcasted somehow from society. Where the bathwater is brown with filth. Anyone that says it's exploitative is just telling you they haven't experienced anything like that in their own lives, in my opinion. But I can tell you that while I haven't experienced that particular midwest flavor of poor, I've experienced adjacent levels. As far as I'm aware Harmony hasn't had that intimate personal growing up poor experience but he captures it when other directors won't because it's not as palatable. Other films will lazily show you the trope of a alcoholic/addict parent and a kid who either rises above it or flees to the freedom they find outside of the home. Gummo stays with the addicts. And it shows you that kids from households like that frequently DON'T rise above it. They're feral. They'll kill cats with BB guns. Why should we pretend that the world is otherwise? It gets into the resentment that builds when you're an outsider and can't find your way in, like the trans sibling that leaves for NYC, while his little brother (who the movie follows) is left behind and goes around calling people homosexual slurs. None of this is exploitative. It's just real (or at times, "hyperreal") and it's sad. And the "Bunny Boy" character which I think often gets forgotten in the discussion in the film, is the moral center, because he is an innocent that is nevertheless mired in it all. How does innocence survive?  
Korine is never judging or poking fun at anyone in this film, it's engaging with the society that creates these conditions.  
  
Similar things can be said of Julien Donkey-Boy, but of mental illness and abuse. Is it exploitative or is it a scenario that is uncomfortable to watch because some things in life are hard and uncomfortable to experience? I think it's also important to note that during both of these films Korine was a drug addict himself and clearly struggling with the sense of alienation and outsiderness that these films also struggle against. Mister Lonely is also a film about mental illness and loneliness and escape, and is where he starts to get more narratively driven. I also believe this is his first film that he made when "clean" and it shows, because although incredibly sad it ends on this note that life is at least worth living if we can make the pain of living a little better for someone else in our lives. Again none of these films are exploitative in my opinion, the subjects are all handled with extreme empathy and care, but they are also handled truthfully and without sanitization.  
  
All that being said, I think the one exception is Kids, which I think does feel a bit exploitative. Or at least gross with no real purpose or meaning. But I think the ick factor comes solely from the real director, Larry Clark who was hanging out at a skatepark and asked an 18 year old boy (Harmony) to write a movie about AIDS.

Right.  

I value peoples' takes if they personally find it exploitative, but most of the popular takes closer to the time of release that had that angle on it seemed to me to be coming from people from other places, particularly New York, who were uniquely insulated from the lives of actual Americans who resemble bits of Gummo.  I personally wasn't dirt poor but I grew up in a small town and there were for sure people around - kids who I was growing up with - who would have been the ones who these critiques were supposed to have been on behalf of.  

They didn't give a fuck.  They liked media like this.  I distinctly remember being over at some latchkey kid's house with "Loser" by Beck on MTV around the same time he threw his family's cat in the dryer, shut the door and threatened to turn it on as a "gag".  Of course, fuck what that guy thought, but the other kids around who were (and in some cases still are as adults, I know some of them) not psychopathic like that were also the ones who were into aggressively confrontational media somewhat regardless if they felt they were the butt of the joke or not.  They were not in the economic or cultural mainstream.  To them, I think a charitable portrayal of their lives, opportunities and challenges would not have looked like presenting them as the morally superior ones, or ending on some contrived positive note or anything like that.  The realistic story was that *that shit sucked* and will probably keep sucking.  It's more courageous of Korine to be showing that - even if it's in a stylized way - than to be stretching it beyond the breaking point to try to change it into something palatable.

Spring Breakers couldn't be more blatantly parody if it had a flashing content warning throughout saying "\*this is a parody*". No idea how you can take it as anything other than that. Yes, it uses a very extreme stylistic approach to get that across, but that's exactly the point.

No one’s saying it isn’t obviously a parody 🙄 But at what point is a fucking parody just DOING THE THING it claims to be criticizing?

I feel like you’d understand, if a move was making a parody/mocking adult men who sexualized kids, but it was full of child actors dressed in clothing meant to sexualize them, behaving in ways that were intended to be provocative. 

It’s not complicated. Something can’t just CALL itself a parody and then we lose the right or ability to think critically about what its actual impact is, what it’s actually accomplishing.
